newsitem.title: USA: N.J. groups oppose new solid waste plan -- paper.
newsitem.headline: N.J. groups oppose new solid waste plan -- paper.

text.p: A New Jersey lawmaker has proposed legislation to deal with the state's solid waste financing crisis, but several groups have already blasted the plan, the Star Ledger reported Tuesday.
New Jersey solid waste facilities are grappling with recent court rulings invalidating a financing system they used to support about $1.6 billion of bonds.

That system forced local communities to send garbage to particular facilities regardless of cheaper alternatives, but the courts said that violated the Interstate Commerce Clause of the U.S. Constitution.

State Assemblyman John Gibson, R-Cape May, proposed a plan that would allow incinerators and waste stations to separate debt service costs from their garbage disposal fees, and allow them to pay off the debt by apportioning the expenses to local governments.
That would help lower fees and let the facilities compete in the new deregulated environment expected to emerge from the court rulings later this year.
But local officials oppose the plan, arguing that the state should pay off the bonds. Environmentalists said the idea would bail out incinerator companies at the expense of taxpayers.
As the legislature grapples with the problem, individual facilities are also trying to get their fees more in line with competitors.

The Union County Utilities Authority, for example, said this week it was negotiating with its incinerator operator to renegotiate its contract. The agency also said it is trying to find a consortium of communities that would guarantee a steady stream of waste for the incinerator, helping it to lower fees.
